system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a male with a history of a right renal transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, was admitted for evaluation and treatment of right renal artery stenosis. He presented with progressive hypertension, and a renal artery duplex suggested stenosis. He was admitted for preoperative hydration and underwent a successful CO2-guided renal arteriogram and stent placement the following day. The procedure was uncomplicated, and his kidney function remained stable postoperatively. He was discharged home the next day in stable condition with instructions to continue immunosuppressive, antihypertensive, and antiplatelet therapies, and to follow up with renal and vascular clinics in two weeks.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Hyperplasia of prostate, unspecified, without urinary obstruction and other lower urinary symptoms (LUTS)
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of bladder

Home

renal artery stenosis
 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.

Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.
 
Discharge Instructions:
Division of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery
Lower Extremity Angioplasty/Stent Discharge Instructions

Medications:
If instructed, take Aspirin 325mg (enteric coated) once daily 
If instructed, take Plavix (Clopidogrel) 75mg once daily
Continue all other medications you were taking before surgery, 
unless otherwise directed
You make take Tylenol or prescribed pain medications for any 
post procedure pain or discomfort

What to expect when you go home:
It is normal to have slight swelling of the legs:
Elevate your leg above the level of your heart (use ___ 
pillows or a recliner) every ___ hours throughout the day and at 
night
Avoid prolonged periods of standing or sitting without your 
legs elevated
It is normal to feel tired and have a decreased appetite, your 
appetite will return with time 
Drink plenty of fluids and eat small frequent meals
It is important to eat nutritious food options (high fiber, 
lean meats, vegetables/fruits, low fat, low cholesterol) to 
maintain your strength and assist in wound healing
To avoid constipation: eat a high fiber diet and use stool 
softener while taking pain medication

What activities you can and cannot do:
When you go home, you may walk and go up and down stairs
You may shower (let the soapy water run over groin incision, 
rinse and pat dry)
Your incision may be left uncovered, unless you have small 
amounts of drainage from the wound, then place a dry dressing or 
band aid over the area that is draining, as needed
No heavy lifting, pushing or pulling (greater than 5 lbs) for 
1 week (to allow groin puncture to heal)
After 1 week, you may resume sexual activity
After 1 week, gradually increase your activities and distance 
walked as you can tolerate
No driving until you are no longer taking pain medications
Call and schedule an appointment to be seen in ___ weeks for 
post procedure check and ultrasound 

What to report to office:
Numbness, coldness or pain in lower extremities 
Temperature greater than 101.5F for 24 hours
New or increased drainage from incision or white, yellow or 
green drainage from incisions
Bleeding from groin puncture site

SUDDEN, SEVERE BLEEDING OR SWELLING (Groin puncture site)
Lie down, keep leg straight and have someone apply firm 
pressure to area for 10 minutes. If bleeding stops, call 
vascular office ___. If bleeding does not stop, call 
___ for transfer to closest Emergency Room. 

 
Followup Instructions:
___

- Other complications due to genitourinary device, implant, and graft
- Kidney replaced by transplant
- Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
- Unspecified essential hypertension
- Pure hypercholesterolemia
- Atherosclerosis of renal artery
- Hyperplasia of prostate, unspecified, without urinary obstruction and other lower urinary symptoms (LUTS)
- Surgical operation with implant of artificial internal device causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication,without mention of misadventure at time of operation
- Personal history of malignant neoplasm of other urinary organs
- Long-term (current) use of insulin

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel, one of the surgical team members. You've been admitted because of a narrowing in the stent that was placed in the artery to your transplanted kidney. We saw this on your recent ultrasound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I remember that ultrasound. My blood pressure’s been going up again. Is that because of the stent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. The ultrasound showed high blood flow speeds—433 and 464 cm/sec—which suggests the stent is narrowing again. That can reduce blood flow to your kidney and raise your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now? Another procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Tomorrow, you’ll have a procedure called angioplasty. We’ll go in through your groin, check the artery with imaging, and reopen the narrowed part of the stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep? Is it risky?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under light sedation—awake but relaxed. It’s generally safe. We’ll monitor your heart and oxygen closely. You’ve had a stent before, so we know your anatomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my kidney—will this help it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, restoring good blood flow should help your kidney function and control your blood pressure better. Your creatinine is 1.8 today—stable, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been taking all my meds—tacrolimus, Cellcept, the blood pressure pills. Should I keep them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep taking them exactly as before. The transplant team checked—your tacrolimus level is stable. That’s important to avoid rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? I’ve been checking my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fingerstick was 178—reasonable. We’ll keep monitoring. You’ll stay on your insulin—Humalog and Lantus—as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the chest X-ray they did earlier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was part of your pre-op check. It showed no heart or lung issues—clear lungs, normal heart size. So you’re cleared for the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. I was worried something else was wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re being thorough. You also had labs—your electrolytes and kidney function are stable. We’ll give you extra fluids tonight to protect your kidney during tomorrow’s procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They mentioned something about a special dye?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use CO2 gas instead of regular contrast dye. It’s safer for your kidney function. We also give bicarbonate and Mucomyst to help protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. Johnson. You’re back from the procedure. Everything went very well. We confirmed the narrowing in the stent and reopened it with a balloon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No complications? How’s the kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No issues. You stayed stable the whole time. Blood flow looks much better now. Your kidney should get the blood it needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll watch it closely. It may improve over the next few days. You’re still on your usual meds—amlodipine, lisinopril, metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel okay—just a little sore at the groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep an eye on the site for any bleeding. You need to keep your leg straight for a few hours to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with light food and advance as you tolerate. Drink plenty of fluids to help flush things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Your vitals are stable—BP 158/72, pulse 64. The transplant team confirmed your tacrolimus level is still in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any infection risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back with low bacteria—less than 10,000—so no infection. You’re on Bactrim, which helps prevent urinary infections anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, for the transplant. I’ve been on that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re not changing your immunosuppression. Everything’s staying the same unless needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your creatinine is still 1.8—no change. That’s excellent after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you’re feeling well. We’ll send you home with instructions. You’ll stay on Plavix and aspirin to keep the stent open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—Plavix 75 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg. Continue all your other meds too. No heavy lifting for a week, and don’t drive while on pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See the vascular clinic in two weeks for a check-up and ultrasound. Call if you have fever, groin swelling, or leg pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your healthy habits—good diet, meds on time, and monitor your blood pressure at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything seems off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You’re doing great.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a male with a history of kidney transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, was admitted for symptomatic in-stent restenosis of the renal artery to his transplanted kidney. He presented with elevated blood pressure, and a transplant kidney ultrasound revealed significantly increased renal artery velocities, confirming restenosis. He underwent elective angioplasty of the existing renal artery stent, which was performed successfully without complications. He remained hemodynamically stable throughout, with no change in kidney function post-procedure. His pain was controlled, and he tolerated a diet advance. He was discharged home in stable condition on day two with continued immunosuppressive, antihypertensive, and antiplatelet therapy, and instructions to follow up with vascular surgery in two weeks.
